```{python}
#|   **Validated coverage sets the upper bound.** In this zero-overhead service-work model, a check that settles more target cases within declared error limits raises the ceiling.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Line plot of review service-cost speedup against validated coverage f on the x-axis. A dashed ceiling curve traces one over one minus f, and three colored cost-ratio curves for 0.01, 0.1, and 0.3 sit below it; an annotated point marks f equals 0.6 capping the speedup at about 2.5x."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _python.plots import COLORS, add_note_box, apply_style

apply_style()

f_grid = [0.95 * i / 399 for i in range(400)]
ratios = [
    {"label": "cost ratio 0.01", "r": 0.01, "color": COLORS["orange"]},
    {"label": "cost ratio 0.1", "r": 0.1, "color": COLORS["green"]},
    {"label": "cost ratio 0.3", "r": 0.3, "color": COLORS["red"]},
]

def s_review(cov, r, a):
    return 1.0 / ((1.0 - cov) + a * r)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.25, 3.12))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.12, right=0.86, top=0.82, bottom=0.28)

ceiling = [1.0 / (1.0 - x) for x in f_grid]
ax.fill_between(f_grid, ceiling, 30, color=COLORS["grid"], alpha=0.35, zorder=0)
ax.text(0.04, 9.0, "unreachable without more validated coverage", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=6.0, color=COLORS["muted"], fontstyle="italic")
ax.plot(f_grid, ceiling, color=COLORS["ink"], linewidth=0.8, linestyle=(0, (4, 3)), zorder=2)

ax.axhline(1.0, color=COLORS["muted"], linewidth=0.7, zorder=1)
ax.text(0.93, 1.04, "no speedup", ha="right", va="bottom", fontsize=6.0, color=COLORS["muted"])

for c in ratios:
    ax.plot(f_grid, [s_review(x, c["r"], x) for x in f_grid], color=c["color"], linewidth=1.9, zorder=3, label=c["label"])
    ax.plot(f_grid, [s_review(x, c["r"], 1.0) for x in f_grid], color=c["color"], linewidth=1.2, linestyle=(0, (2, 2)), zorder=3)

ax.scatter([0.6], [2.5], marker="o", s=22, facecolor=COLORS["note_fill"], edgecolor=COLORS["ink"], linewidth=1.3, zorder=4)
ax.text(0.58, 2.95, "f = 0.6 caps the speedup at 2.5x", ha="right", va="bottom", fontsize=6.0, color=COLORS["ink"])

ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(0, 0.95)
ax.set_ylim(0.7, 30)
ax.set_xlabel("validated coverage f  (share of cases settled without escalation)", fontsize=7)
ax.set_ylabel("review service-work speedup", fontsize=7)
ax.set_xticks([0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8])
ax.set_yticks([1, 2, 5, 10, 20])
ax.set_yticklabels(["1x", "2x", "5x", "10x", "20x"], fontsize=6.4)
ax.tick_params(axis="both", length=2.5, width=0.6, pad=2, labelsize=6.4)
ax.grid(axis="both", color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.5, zorder=0)

for spine in ["top", "right"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["left"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])
ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])

legend = ax.legend(
    loc="lower left",
    bbox_to_anchor=(0.0, 1.02),
    fontsize=6.0,
    frameon=True,
    facecolor="white",
    edgecolor="white",
    framealpha=0.92,
    handlelength=1.6,
    borderpad=0.15,
    labelspacing=0.3,
    ncol=1,
)
for text in legend.get_texts():
    text.set_color(COLORS["ink"])

add_note_box(
    fig,
    "Solid curves show an ideal router that pays for the cheap check only where it settles the case (a = f); dashed color curves screen every candidate (a = 1). The black dashed line is the free-check ceiling 1/(1-f).",
    xywh=(0.10, 0.03, 0.80, 0.11),
    fontsize=5.5,
)

plt.show()
plt.close(fig)
```

When we set the $\epsilon = 0$ ceiling, we isolate our validated coverage from routing, auditing, and rework overheads (@fig-rejection-bound-ceiling). Our solid curves represent an ideal scenario where we pay for the cheap check only when it successfully settles the comparison, while the corresponding dashed curves assume we pay to screen cases that subsequently escalate. Remember, every comparison falling outside our validated coverage still incurs the full compiler-connected RTL reference cost. At $f = 0.6$, even a hypothetical free check cannot push our speedup past 2.5x in this model. Consequently, when we claim a screening-work speedup, we must explicitly provide the cost ratio, the class-specific error bounds, and the rigorous sampling and confidence calculations backing our coverage estimate. For any consequential architectural decision, we should always report a conservative lower confidence bound on our supported coverage (derived under a predeclared target sampling procedure) rather than relying solely on a fragile point estimate of $f$.

We must also recognize that this component-level bound does not predict our iteration time or our complete-workflow productivity. Queueing delays, parallel simulation capacity, raw model and tool licensing costs, failed run overheads, and human review cycles all sit squarely outside this specific service-work model. Finally, we must ensure that each transferred result remains strictly attached to the exact hardware and software versions it observed during evaluation.

## Version Dependencies

When we transfer a hardware-software result, we must recognize that its validity hinges entirely on the specific version pair that produced it. If we change either the hardware snapshot (such as NPU tensor array dimensions or CPU ISA extension configs) or the software stack (such as Triton 3.0 compiler passes or LLVM 19 lowering targets), that invariant may immediately fail. We simply cannot requalify one side of the system without rigidly recording the other, as doing so destroys the foundation needed to support our target claims.

Any target we evaluate naturally widens our causal chain from a single array parameter out to the compiler, runtime environment, memory hierarchy, and host system. Because of this sprawling dependency, we must version our hardware and software snapshots together. Furthermore, we need to continuously check our local, subsystem-level objectives against our overarching Lighthouse system goals to ensure they remain aligned.

We often find that a single-layer optimization can be locally correct while actively degrading the complete system. In modern cross-layer architecture, our work routinely involves techniques like algorithmic tiling optimized for the memory hierarchy [@DaoEtAl2022FlashAttention] and aggressively pairing narrow numerical formats with both hardware efficiency and accuracy objectives [@RouhaniEtAl2023Microscaling]. Take our Lighthouse system as an example. Both the compute capability (RVV vector units or NPU tensor array) and the camera-interface bandwidth must work together to support the target frame rate. If we rigidly hold either the hardware or software fixed, we artificially restrict our design space and mask critical tradeoffs that a joint design approach would expose. Ultimately, a localized throughput improvement that violates our strict latency or bandwidth constraints remains completely unacceptable.

The performance benefits we extract from these cross-layer techniques remain tightly bound to the paired algorithm, chosen numerical format, spatial mapping, software stack (Triton, LLVM), and underlying hardware conditions. The moment we change any single member of this stack, we must reopen and re-verify all of our dependent latency, bandwidth, accuracy, and efficiency claims.

When our software tools return performance signals, those results only support our target claim after we rigorously qualify the tests, profiles, and failure data against our precise hardware snapshot and study scope. This careful interpretation is what transforms raw data into actionable feedback for our next architectural decision. Because software tuning typically converges much faster than hardware implementation checks, we must bind these two evaluation paths with a shared study record. When we keep them joined, we ensure the rapid software iteration path never bypasses or overwrites our essential, slower hardware validation checks (@fig-hardware-software-coevolution).

![**Hardware and software versions bound the result.** We must evolve our hardware target state and software path state together through a shared study record. While a fast software result may propose a hardware revision, we cannot allow it to replace our slower hardware checks or alter the target state without a formal review.](images/F9c-hardware-software-coevolution){#fig-hardware-software-coevolution width="100%" fig-alt="Two-lane diagram in which the software path can propose a hardware revision, while a shared study record and decision-holder review determine whether target state changes."}

Our hardware target deliberately exposes legal architectural knobs to the software interface, just as our generated kernels and compiler schedules often reveal intense pressure to revise the hardware snapshot itself. Notice that the arrow labeled "proposed revision" in our diagram does not change the target state directly. Instead, our shared study record and decision-holder review determine whether that proposed revision actually becomes the new target state. The two outer return paths carry only those accepted, reviewed revisions back to our versioned hardware target and software interface. Consequently, an unexpected fast software result can reopen a crucial hardware design question without silently overwriting our established baseline.

Importantly, our figure does not mandate a synchronized, lock-step universal loop. We understand that our hardware and software teams will naturally advance at different rates. Instead, we enforce that each evaluation result remains strictly bound to an immutable hardware-software version pair. Our review process then joins only those claims whose architectural dependencies intersect, rather than forcing us to serialize every minor change through a single fixed development cycle.

In this methodology, we define the software state comprehensively to include the compiler (Triton, LLVM), runtime environment, programming interface, and all generated machine artifacts. If our execution target relies on drivers, deeply embedded firmware, operating-system services, or device control logic, we must strictly version those elements within the exact same lane.

Our design-time results, production telemetry, and subsequent software enablement phases are rigorously scoped to the artifact versions and operating conditions they actually observe; therefore, they support entirely different architectural claims. A simulator result explicitly belongs to the candidate design and conditions we evaluated at that moment. Production telemetry belongs exclusively to the shipped hardware-software version and the live deployed workload. Furthermore, any later compiler or firmware result belongs strictly to its revised software path and the specific hardware version it targets. Our study record binds these returns together while keeping them separately scoped, guaranteeing that a newer optimization signal never silently overwrites an older, foundational result.

When we execute a rollback, we must restore the entire configured dependency set (not just our isolated model weights or software binaries). If a memory schema, numerical representation, compiler, runtime, interface, tool, library, or hardware target has changed, simply returning to an earlier learned component without its exact compatible configuration utterly fails to restore our earlier system state.

Attributed observations from deployment can strongly motivate a new calibration study for our next hardware generation, but they must never automatically update a surrogate model or an architectural design rule. As predictive-uncertainty evaluations demonstrate, accuracy and calibration easily degrade under dataset shift [@OvadiaEtAl2019UncertaintyShift]. While this degradation motivates us to implement new target checks, it does not magically establish architecture correctness, nor does it transfer a complete architecture conclusion. Our calibration study must explicitly bind each observation to the shipped hardware, the exact software stack, the workload cohort, and our measurement conditions. We must keep our calibration cases completely separate from our held-out checks, and meticulously test whether the deployed cohort actually covers our next architectural target. We have to remember that the deployed workload is merely a selected sample of what the earlier system happened to serve. When we reuse a learned predictor, any changed workload or operating-condition distribution becomes a textbook architecture instance of distribution shift. If we fit a model to that shift without rigorous checks, we risk foolishly narrowing our next processor design around yesterday's traffic.

For instance, NVIDIA reported workload-specific single-node training improvements on the exact same H100 hardware between the MLPerf Training v2.1 preview and v3.0 simply by applying software optimizations, which yielded a 17 percent BERT improvement [@EassaEryilmaz2023H100MLPerfSoftware]. We must view this vendor-reported comparison strictly as an example of continuing software enablement; it does not represent a dependable, compounding improvement rate, nor does it revise our hardware's fundamental design-time result.

Ultimately, our five-step transfer test is what safely transforms these complex source-to-target differences into a rigorous new architectural target study.

## Framing Transfer Studies

When we apply these five steps to our Lighthouse target, we uncover a fresh design problem, a specific set of unit actions, and the remaining target checks we need to satisfy.

1. **Compare the decisions and identify the changes.** Our source study compared five simulated array shapes against a fixed local score. The 32-by-32 shape tied with the 16-by-64 configuration and emerged as our local reference and technical recommendation. However, our target environment asks a fundamentally different question. Should we freeze an RTL-facing array alongside its software and memory interfaces? Here, the workload shift is distributional, while the integration of a new compiler (Triton, LLVM), RTL, memory hierarchies, and physical paths introduces sweeping component changes. Because these shifts overlap (and because our artifact boundaries and acceptance criteria have evolved) the target carries entirely new decision semantics. We are facing a completely new architectural design problem, not merely a selective requalification of an old source decision.
2. **Separate the source into transfer units.** We must break down the source into modular transfer units. Elements like the historical record, workload, represented state, proposing methods, our SCALE-Sim screen, tool interfaces, candidate artifacts, and final conclusions all carry distinct invariants and architectural dependencies.
3. **Identify the affected slice.** We see immediate divergence in the trace-backed workload, mapping strategies, executable paths, process libraries, physical validation checks, and overarching system objectives. While our source simulator outputs remain valid as historical data, they completely miss the new properties introduced by our target architecture.
4. **Assign an action to each unit.** We must decisively route each unit by reusing historical artifacts, refreshing the workload and project state; re-evaluate the target alternatives; requalify our screening tools, recalibrating them only if their underlying semantics hold up. Furthermore, we must adapt our interfaces and architectural checks, retrain any learned component only if it currently lacks support, and recompose the target system wherever usable units demand new integrations. Ultimately, we must replace or retire incompatible components, and firmly reject any direct transfer of the local score and source recommendation.
5. **Require target evidence and test any claim of transfer benefit.** We must back every changed dependency with a check capable of observing its specific architectural risk. Similarly, any unchanged component interfacing with a modified neighbor demands a rigorous integration check. If our study claims a transfer benefit for an adapted component, we must prove it by comparing against a strict target-only baseline. We have to retire any harmful source prior. A cost-neutral prior offers no transfer benefit and only survives if it demonstrably improves another declared target criterion.

While these five steps beautifully define our target study, they do not give us the authority to freeze an array or an interface. Until we explicitly declare our legal target candidate set and establish a credible architectural comparator, we cannot run our target comparison. As a result, our target decision remains wide open.

We cannot simply inherit claims of representativeness, implementation readiness, physical viability, or operational success from the source array's results. Instead, each shifted dependency generates a minimum target test and strictly bounds what we can claim if we skip that test (@tbl-ch9-target-tests). We must treat these obligations as unique requirements for our specific target decision, not as items on some universal signoff checklist.

| **Target obligation** | **Minimum test** | **Boundary if absent** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Workload coverage** | We require trace-backed common and tail cases, strictly versioned and with all exclusions clearly stated. | We can make no representativeness claim. |
| **Candidate comparison** | We must predeclare the legal target space, search and evaluation budgets, a credible architecture comparator, our decision rule, and a robust sensitivity or resolving-power check. | We can make no claims outside our evaluated candidates, nor any comparative AI-contribution claim if our study cannot distinguish its arms. |
| **Transfer benefit** | When we claim that transfer helps, we must compare the adapted component against a target-only arm sharing the same tasks, data, tool access, budgets, and stopping rules (without the source unit). We must explicitly count adaptation, requalification, integration, use, checking, and retirement costs. | We forfeit any transfer-benefit claim. We must retire a harmful source prior, retaining a cost-neutral one only if it improves another declared target criterion. |
| **Mapping and software path** | We demand compiler-generated (Triton, LLVM), end-to-end execution using pinned mappings, compilers, runtimes, CPU ISA extension configs (RVV), driver and firmware versions (where applicable), and strictly defined interface versions. | We cannot claim our array is usable by the target software stack. |
| **Interface and memory cost** | We must measure offload granularity, bandwidth, traffic, and latency using LogCA and Roofline models, alongside a calibrated energy-and-power model that captures execution rates, duty cycles, leakage, idle power, and the complete subsystem boundary. | We forfeit any 3\ W power or system-speedup claims. |
| **Cheap-screen validity** | We must check representative target samples against a separate property-specific reference path (gem5, Verilator), enforcing class-specific error limits, uncertainty measures, the ability to decline unsupported predictions, and a subsequent drift audit. | We relegate SCALE-Sim to a source-study tool rather than a valid target decision filter. |
| **RTL behavior** | We need independently derived reference tests where practical, alongside lint, functional simulation, synthesis, and formal checks. We must also add fault and threat models specifically required by our target architecture. | We can make no implementation-readiness, reliability, or security claims beyond the specific properties we checked. |
| **Physical behavior** | We must pin our 3\ nm-class low-power process design kit, libraries, and PVT conditions; then we test area and floorplan feasibility, setup and hold corners, congestion, routed dynamic and leakage power, power delivery, and electrothermal behavior. | We surrender any signoff, tapeout, or physical-feasibility claims. |
| **Containment** | We must exercise every proposed bypass, disable function, guardband, isolation mechanism, or fallback against the specific fault or attack it is designed to contain. | We cannot claim that our implementation will contain or recover from that failure. |
| **Operational readiness** | We must confirm required tool access, have our qualified operators challenge representative target cases within our allocated review capacity, and permanently record our named decision authority. | We cannot claim that our transferred workflow is operable, challengeable, or capable of supporting a target commitment. |

: **Each obligation changes what our next evaluation must measure.** We ensure that untested boundaries remain fully visible in our architectural analysis, rather than allowing them to be absorbed into a generalized claim. {#tbl-ch9-target-tests tbl-colwidths="[22,46,32]"}

Our workload coverage and candidate comparisons ultimately frame the target architecture question. The concept of transfer benefit stands separate; we apply it only when our study argues that transferring a source structure provides a tangible advantage over building a target-only version. If we claim that an AI-assisted workflow gives us an edge, we must back it up with the matched, complete-workflow comparison detailed in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect. From there, our executable paths and interface costs prove whether our candidate architecture can actually run. Finally, our cheap-screen, RTL, physical, containment, and operational-readiness checks draw strict boundaries around what our target results can legitimately support.

We can see how this architectural reasoning scales beyond our initial array study by examining three compact transfer cases (@tbl-ch9-transfer-stress-tests). For each case, we isolate the transfer unit, identify the shifting dependency, prescribe a valid action, and mandate a rigorous target check. We chose these cases to represent deliberately diverse scenarios across the design space. The first is a transfer case we constructed ourselves. While CircuitNet supplies congestion-prediction data and tasks [@ChaiEtAl2022CircuitNet], and ChiPBench offers end-to-end physical placement and PPA evaluations [@WangEtAl2025ChiPBench], neither source natively reports the combined transfer procedure we outline here. Our other two cases tackle the realities of continuing software optimization on fixed hardware, and a stark physical silicon defect that no software patch could ever resolve.

| **Transfer unit** | **Changed dependency** | **Valid action** | **Required target check** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Our constructed transfer case for a learned congestion predictor trained on one specific process, library, and design family | Our target process, standard cell library, netlist family, placement flow, or routed-result definition shifts. | We must first requalify the unchanged predictor; we only recalibrate, adapt, retrain, or retire it after isolating exactly what no longer holds. | We must measure class-specific target errors and decision quality against routed target results that we keep strictly isolated from our calibration or training data. |
| H100 software-optimization results reported between MLPerf Training v2.1 preview and v3.0 [@EassaEryilmaz2023H100MLPerfSoftware] | A subsequent compiler (Triton, LLVM), library, workload, or hardware generation alters our paired configuration. | We must constrain the published improvement to its explicitly reported versions and workloads; we then rerun the comparison for our new architectural pair. | We must repeat the end-to-end workload measurement, explicitly pinning both hardware and software versions while maintaining the exact same result definition. |
| Cougar Point containment and correction results [@Intel2011CougarPoint] | Our target defect and the specific mechanisms capable of reaching it differ. Intel's permanent correction required revised silicon alongside repair or replacement; they did not present a firmware-only fix. | We cannot assume a firmware-only remedy will resolve a deep silicon defect; we must deploy a correction or containment mechanism structurally matched to the failure. | We must exercise the corrected silicon and any proposed containment strategies against our target failure class before we ever claim a correction. |

: **The same transfer test applies to our learned, software, and physical components.** Our actions directly follow the changed dependencies, and our target checks must rigorously observe the specific failures or improvements we claim. {#tbl-ch9-transfer-stress-tests tbl-colwidths="[24,29,23,24]"}

When examining the learned-predictor case, we ensure that a familiar model name never blindly substitutes for rigorous target support. Our H100 case preserves the integrity of the reported result, stopping us from improperly extrapolating a specific 17 percent gain into a generalized software-improvement rate. Meanwhile, the Cougar Point case drives home critical lessons about failure reach, reminding us that we cannot assume every silicon defect will succumb to the same architectural remedy. Across all three examples, we successfully retain valuable source knowledge while strictly refusing to stretch our conclusions beyond the specific configurations that produced them.

Importantly, transferring these components does not alter our core decision rights. While we allow automated components to propose or screen candidates within the boundaries of our declared study, the heavy responsibilities (rejections, waivers, the final architecture freeze, physical signoff, and tapeout) remain firmly in the hands of the named architectural roles we defined in @sec-what-architect-owns.

At this stage, our adaptation decision is complete, even though our ultimate target architecture decision remains unresolved. We have effectively paved the way for our study structure and reference candidate to move forward. However, the original source conclusion simply cannot make that leap with us.

## Common Architectural Pitfalls

When we adapt legacy microarchitectures, analytical surrogate models, and offload patterns into new system contexts without explicit transfer contracts, we introduce severe architectural risks. As we execute design transfers, we frequently fall into critical traps regarding conclusion transferability, LogCA offload bounds, requalification scopes, and selective surrogate math.

**Transferring Source Conclusions Without Requalifying Target Artifacts.** Assuming that a performance win, optimization ratio, or trade-off conclusion validated on a source process node or workload automatically holds in a new target context. While source candidate identities and execution scripts can be transferred, microarchitectural conclusions do not transfer across boundary shifts in standard cell libraries, ISA lowerings such as Triton to RVV 1.0, or memory controllers.

**Violating LogCA Offload Bounds in Accelerator Design.** Evaluating host-to-accelerator offload patterns using simplified execution speedup estimates while ignoring LogCA communication constraints [@AltafWood2017LogCA].[^fn-logca-offload-c09] Architectural models that omit latency, overhead, communication gap, and bus contention across PCIe or CXL interconnects yield unrealistic offload efficiency metrics, concealing DMA setup costs and host-side synchronization stalls.

[^fn-logca-offload-c09]: **LogCA offload bounds**: The LogCA performance model [@AltafWood2017LogCA] bounds host-accelerator offload efficiency using four hardware parameters: fixed invocation overhead ($o$), work payload ($g$), acceleration factor ($A$), and communication gap ($b$). Total execution time $T_{\mathrm{acc}} = o + g/A + bg$ demonstrates that offload speedup is achievable only when payload size $g$ is large enough to amortize host-side launch latency ($o$) and bus transfer penalties ($bg$) across PCIe or CXL interconnects.

**Conflating Limited Requalification with Decision Reformulation.** Failing to distinguish between updating dependent checks under localized drift versus reformulating a fundamentally altered design decision. Treating shifted objective semantics or new packaging constraints as minor parameter drift leads to improper model recalibration, while treating minor workload adjustments as ground-up redesigns wastes compute on redundant verification.

**Misapplying Selective Classification Math to Cheap-Screen Surrogates.** Utilizing fast learned surrogates for candidate screening without establishing rigorous selective classification coverage and error bounds [@ElYanivWiener2010SelectiveClassification].[^fn-selective-classification-c09] Evaluating cheap proxy models without defining explicit abstain thresholds or computing coverage-dependent error rates causes surrogates to issue high-confidence predictions in out-of-distribution design regions, steering candidate selection toward flawed microarchitectures.

[^fn-selective-classification-c09]: **Selective classification theory**: Selective classification theory [@ElYanivWiener2010SelectiveClassification] formalizes prediction with an abstain option via a selection function $g(x) \in \{0, 1\}$. In microarchitectural surrogate screening, configuring an explicit abstain threshold allows the cheap proxy model to reject candidates in low-confidence or out-of-distribution regions, falling back to full-fidelity reference evaluation ($c_{\mathrm{hi}}$) to bound false-positive acceptances of unfeasible designs.

**Evaluating Transfer Benefit Against Unmatched Baselines.** Claiming architectural improvement from an AI-assisted or transferred workflow by comparing it against an unoptimized or mismatched target baseline. An authentic transfer evaluation requires comparing the ported design against an equally tuned target-only baseline while fully accounting for adaptation overhead, verification contracts, and physical signoff costs.

## Open Questions in Architectural Transfer

The true frontier of architecture reuse lies not in the mechanics of packaging components, but in rigorously bounding their expiration. As we have established throughout our discussions, physical implementations, software stacks (Triton, LLVM), and integration constraints inevitably shift between design problems. When left unchecked, this architectural drift turns reuse into a source of silent system failure rather than an efficiency gain. The open problems we outline here define the very edge of our current capabilities. They ask how we can mathematically and empirically isolate the precise slice of a system that requires requalification when a dependency breaks, without indiscriminately discarding unaffected prior work. Solving these dependency and qualification challenges is absolutely essential for building autonomous design systems that scale. Until we can automatically resolve when a prior architectural conclusion has expired and safely transfer verified state, manual requalification will remain our primary bottleneck. Consequently, each of these questions targets a systemic barrier to scalable, AI-assisted architecture design. They offer substantial, self-contained opportunities for a dissertation or major research program to fundamentally change how we trust and transfer technical artifacts.

**Scoping requalification.** Our first major challenge is determining *how much* of the system we actually need to re-test (or requalify) without accidentally preserving stale architectural claims or, worse, solving the wrong design problem entirely.

- **How can we identify the minimal safe set of components to requalify after a hardware or software change?** Hidden dependencies can easily make a partial re-test look sufficient while leaving an invalid architectural claim completely untouched. An AI-assisted architecture system must be capable of mapping complex system-wide dependencies to pinpoint the exact subset of claims affected by a given change. This capability would allow us to achieve the safety of full cross-layer requalification while requiring only a fraction of the target checking.

- **At what point does a system change create an entirely new design problem rather than just requiring limited requalification?** A shifted objective or a new set of design constraints can completely invalidate our original design question, even if many of the underlying artifacts still match. We need reliable methodologies to help architects determine exactly which prior claims remain relevant, and when a change is so fundamental that it demands a newly formulated design study from the ground up.

**Predicting useful transfer.** Before moving any components, our design systems must determine whether a transferred component will actually improve the target design decision enough to justify the heavy lifting of requalification and integration.

- **Which invariants truly predict whether a learned architecture component is worth transferring?** Simply looking at a model's accuracy on the source task is rarely enough, because preserved behavior can still silently fail under changed target conditions. As researchers and architects, we need robust invariants that can reliably predict target decision quality and estimate requalification costs far better than naive metrics like source accuracy or basic source-target similarity.

- **How can we efficiently detect interaction failures when a transferred component meets a changed interface?** A transferred component might perfectly retain its local behavior, yet silently fail because the surrounding architectural environment (such as the compiler-to-ISA mapping, the RTL-to-memory contract, or a critical timing assumption) has shifted. We need smarter, more aggressive detectors that can catch these integration failures without forcing architects and engineers to manually repeat every single verification check from the source system.

## Conclusion

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Transfer components, not conclusions"}
**Rule 1. Preserve Invariants.** Reuse a data source, model, interface, tool path, or check strictly while its invariants and dependencies hold for the target.

**Rule 2. Force Requalification.** Requalify any claim affected by a changed workload, software version, library, process condition, interface, objective, or constraint.

**Rule 3. Enforce Integration Checks.** Mandate a new integration check whenever an unchanged component interfaces with a changed neighbor.

**Rule 4. Isolate Conclusions.** Carry the source record forward, but explicitly withhold or narrow its conclusion until newly established target evidence supports it.
:::

Our five-step transfer methodology begins by explicitly comparing the source and target design decisions, subsequently partitioning the original system into granular units to identify the precise slice affected by our changes. From there, we assign a definitive action to each unit before independently evaluating the underlying evidence. We mandate a rigorous target check for every modified component, and if we claim that the transfer process itself provides a tangible architectural advantage, we demand a strict target-only baseline comparison. Ultimately, our approach avoids both lazy blanket reuse and wasteful blanket repetition. Instead, we generate a rigorous, component-specific accounting of which design invariants remain structurally valid and what fresh experimental evidence our target still requires.

When we apply this framework to the Lighthouse target study across all 8 prompt stack layers, we treat the retained simulator telemetry and candidate design identities strictly as historical baselines. We carry forward the 32x32 spatial configuration merely as a historical reference point; meanwhile, we systematically refresh the XRBench / SPEC2026 / MLPerf workload alongside the RV64GCV ISA contract, Triton JIT to RVV 1.0 lowering toolchain, Ramulator DRAM timing models, TSMC N7 process parameters, 3\ W TDP power envelope, UPF IEEE 1801 power domains, and SVA/BMC formal verification checks, measuring both executable and physical implementation pathways, and selectively requalifying SCALE-Sim solely for those target cases it can reliably screen within declared error margins. Consequently, the earlier local performance scores, failed analytical explanations, initial AI-contribution comparisons, and originally recorded design recommendations explicitly do not transfer into our final RTL implementation decisions.

As we transition into the next chapter, we hand off this rigorously defined source-to-target map, our tightly versioned hardware-software state, and the remaining target integration checks (@sec-evaluating-agentic-architect). Armed with this foundation, we pivot to a fundamentally different evaluation. Across repeated and highly varied architectural studies, does our configured system actually improve the final hardware result, reduce the total engineering cost of achieving it, or successfully deliver on both fronts?
